extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, poets, and educated readers interested in principles of literary criticism and creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards and evaluative criteria for criticism and for creative literary work (especially poetry), as articulated in Matthew Arnold's Essays in Criticism. Focuses on what makes good criticism and what makes creative writing durable and valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The function of criticism: see the object 'as in itself it really is'
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the business of the critical power ... in all branches of knowledge, ... to see the object as in itself it really is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism's central duty is clear, objective apprehension of the literary/artistic object. The critic should aim at an impartial, dispassionate vision which clarifies the thing under examination rather than distorting it by personal or partisan aims. This function grounds the critic's role in preparing the intellectual materials for creative work and in establishing an order of ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should be disinterested and avoid false or malicious judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold repeats Wordsworth's warning about "false or malicious criticism" and insists that such criticism "had better never have been written."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must not write out of spite, envy, or partisan motive. False or malicious reviews harm readers' minds and the intellectual atmosphere; good criticism requires honesty, moral responsibility, and avoidance of personal attacks. Competent criticism seeks truth, not triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic must be competent: a man of letters, not merely a friend or relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A competent critic should be "a man of letters, not, as too often happens, some relation or friend with no qualification for his task except affection for his author."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical authority depends on genuine qualification — learning, judgement, and literary competence. Introductions and critical notices should be written by qualified critics rather than by unqualified admirers; otherwise guidance to readers is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical work is preparatory: it supplies the materials and order of ideas for creative genius
rubrics_metrics.description: "The critical power ... tends, at last, to make an intellectual situation of which the creative power can profitably avail itself ... it tends to establish an order of ideas ... and make the best ideas prevail."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism is valuable because it forms the intellectual atmosphere and supplies ideas that creative writers synthesize. Good criticism prepares society and artists with the ideas and perspectives necessary for lasting creative achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative genius is chiefly synthesis and exposition, not discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: "The grand work of literary genius is a work of synthesis and exposition, not of analysis and discovery; the gift lies in the faculty of being happily inspired by a certain intellectual and spiritual atmosphere..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetry or literature, measure how well the work combines, organizes, and presents prevailing ideas and life—not merely whether it invents wholly new philosophical doctrines. Enduring works often synthesize and illuminate the current intellectual climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: A poet/writer must 'know life and the world' — breadth and thoroughness of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "A poet, for instance, ought to know life and the world before dealing with them in poetry ... the creation of a modern poet, to be worth much, implies a great critical effort behind it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess creative works for richness of matter, variety, and comprehensiveness in representing life. Poets who lack sufficient acquaintance with the ideas and realities of their time risk producing works that are premature, empty, or short-lived (Arnold cites Byron and Shelley as examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and cultivate the critical habit: learning sustains creative excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold argues that Goethe's endurance came from "the complete culture and unfettered thinking of a large body of Germans" and that reading and wide learning can constitute an equivalent atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both critics and creative writers should cultivate broad reading and culture. When national intellectual life is lacking, extensive learning and criticism can create the supportive atmosphere for lasting literary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism ought to be measured, modest, and avoid ex cathedra pronouncements
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold disclaims "assertions issued ex cathedra" and warns against critics saddling their university or office with responsibility for their personal views; he also withdraws over-vivacious phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid grandstanding, authoritative airs, and institutional posturing. Modesty and personal accountability are preferred to appealing to institutional sanction; vigorous language should not substitute for sound argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish creative and critical rank but recognize criticism's necessary role
rubrics_metrics.description: "The critical power is of lower rank than the creative. True; but ... the exercise of the creative power ... is not at all epochs and under all conditions possible ... the creative power must have elements, materials; what if it has not those materials?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While original creation ranks higher, criticism plays an indispensable role: it prepares, supplies ideas, and disciplines thought. Evaluation frameworks should respect the primacy of creation but credit criticism for enabling creative epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should aim at 'truth by comparison' — make better ideas prevail
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold: criticism "tends to establish an order of ideas, if not absolutely true, yet true by comparison with that which it displaces; to make the best ideas prevail."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should judge comparatively: propose better readings/ideas that improve upon prevailing misconceptions. Absolute final truth may be unattainable, but criticism's worth lies in improving understanding relative to prior errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan or purely practical/political imperatives in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold contrasts French intellectual impulses to force ideas into immediate politics with English practicalness; he warns against imposing one's "right" upon others and against criticism that serves party catchwords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical judgment should be led by ideas and literary values rather than political aims, party loyalties, or immediate practical agendas. Critics must be careful not to conflate intellectual evaluation with political advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination: critics should ask what real service their criticism does
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold urges critics to "try his own conscience, and for asking himself of what real service at any given moment the practice of criticism either is or may be made to his own mind and spirit, and to the minds and spirits of others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before writing criticism, practitioners should consider the constructive contribution of their work — whether it enlightens readers, prepares creators, or simply indulges personal preference. This moral and professional self-scrutiny is part of good critical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism can be a legitimate form of creative fulfilment for many
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold notes that creative fulfilment can be found "in well-doing, in learning, they may have it even in criticising" and that not all can be original creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating careers or outputs, acknowledge criticism as a valuable intellectual vocation. Quality is judged by conscience, rigor, and contribution, not solely by whether one produces original masterpieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and comparative perspective strengthens judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold repeatedly uses historical comparisons (Greece, Renaissance, Goethe, Burke, the French Revolution) to show how critical and creative epochs differ and to explain literary durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism employs historical and cross-cultural comparison to situate works, trace intellectual lineage, and judge endurance. Critics should weigh works against wider historical standards and analogues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate creative works for completeness of intellectual 'materials' and readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold argues many early 19th-century English works were "premature" because they lacked sufficient data and materials; creative works must have both the creative power and the right moment/atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work has adequate intellectual grounding: sufficient facts, ideas, and maturity of thought. A work may be brilliant in energy but fail to endure if it lacks completeness and variety of matter.
